title: Citi Joins US Banks Restricting AI Agents From Customer Accounts
excerpt: JPMorgan and Charles Schwab have drawn the same line this week: outside AI agents may look at balances, but they may not move money.
body:
• Citigroup has become the latest major US bank to restrict third-party AI agents from accessing customer accounts, the Financial Times reported, citing security, liability and deposit-flight concerns.
  • JPMorgan Chase and Charles Schwab have taken the same line this week: outside agents may not move customers' money.
  • The practical rule for customers: an AI assistant connected through a data provider may be able to show balances, but it cannot pay bills or transfer funds at these banks.
  • Banks say the alternative is their own controlled tools and authenticated channels — not agents logging in with your password.

Citigroup has become the latest large US bank to restrict third-party artificial intelligence agents from accessing customer accounts, the Financial Times reported, as the industry draws a common line against autonomous software moving money on a customer's behalf. The concerns behind the restrictions, as summarised in coverage of the FT report, are security, liability and deposit flight — the fear that an agent which can see every account could quickly shift large balances to higher-yielding rivals.

Citi's move follows public statements this week from the two ends of American finance. JPMorgan Chase chief executive Jamie Dimon told investors on the bank's earnings call that it will not allow just any outside agent inside the company, calling the risk to clients and the bank too high and warning against rogue agents. A JPMorgan spokesperson confirmed external agents are blocked from acting for retail customers, while customer-authorised data sharing through open-banking providers remains supported.

Schwab: tens of blocks a week, not hundreds

Charles Schwab chief executive Rick Wurster told Bloomberg TV on Friday that his firm is actively blocking unauthorised AI agents attempting to move clients' money, including Meta's Muse, according to Gizmodo's report of the interview and Bloomberg Law's coverage. His objection was control and liability: a customer handing a password to an agent creates actions neither the firm nor the client can control, leaving open who is responsible when something goes wrong.

https://x.com/rohanpaul_ai/status/2111145441421312174

Wurster also gave a sense of scale. He receives weekly reports on detected and rejected agent attempts, and the numbers run in the tens per week for the large agents — not yet into the hundreds. His reading was that customers like AI but are not yet willing to hand their financial accounts over to it. Schwab is preparing controlled connections for external models through authenticated servers, but with a hard limit: agents may view balances and do research; they will not be allowed to move money. The firm is meanwhile promoting its own in-house assistant, which handles administrative and informational tasks rather than trading.

Why banks are moving together

Three pressures explain the timing. First, fraud: an agent holding credentials is a scalable attack surface, and a compromised agent could repeat a mistake or a malicious instruction across many accounts. Second, liability: banking law has no settled answer for who bears a loss when a customer's own agent initiates a bad transfer. Third, economics: low-cost deposits are a core profit engine, and an agent that automatically hunts yield threatens them directly — a risk bank analysts have flagged since agent products topped app-store charts in September.

None of this is a rejection of AI inside the banks themselves. JPMorgan is building its own cash-management automation, Schwab has its in-house assistant, and lenders are working on agent-safety tooling with technology partners. The distinction the industry is enforcing is between AI the bank controls, inside its own authentication and audit systems, and outside agents arriving with a customer's password.

What this means for customers

For now, expect a consistent experience across the largest US banks: personal AI assistants can increasingly read — summarising balances, transactions and holdings through authorised data connections — but they cannot act. Paying a bill, sending a transfer or sweeping cash to a higher-yield account still requires the bank's own app or a channel the bank can authenticate and audit. That boundary may soften if agent-identity standards, of the kind Meta says it is developing with partners, give banks a way to verify an agent and its permissions. Until then, if an agent asks for your banking password, the banks' answer — now including Citi's — is that the request itself is the red flag.
